prompt: Which part of Google Cloud does this course's lab answer the way the service itself would?
hint: Google ships an emulator for a handful of data services, and one of them comes with the CLI.

choices.text: Projects and folders, through Terraform
choices.why: Terraform plans projects and folders, and contacts nobody to do it. A plan is not an answer from Google.

choices.text: Pub/Sub, through the emulator that ships with the CLI
choices.why: Right. Pub/Sub is the one service in the lab with something on your computer answering its API.

choices.text: IAM, through the emulator's permission checks
choices.why: The emulator says at start-up that IAM integration is disabled. It checks no permission at all.

choices.text: Compute Engine, through `gcloud compute`
choices.why: With no emulator for it, `gcloud compute` sends its requests to Google, which refuses the placeholder.

prompt: A section of this course shows a `terraform plan` that adds a firewall rule. What has that plan proved?
hint: Ask who answered: Google, or a program on the laptop.

choices.text: That Google would create the rule if the plan were applied
choices.why: Nothing in a plan asks Google. A policy, a quota or a missing permission is found only when the request is sent.

choices.text: That the rule exists in the project `planner-dev`
choices.why: A plan creates nothing. It says what Terraform would ask for, and nothing was asked.

choices.text: Nothing, since a plan is output invented by the course
choices.why: The plan is a real answer from a real program, run in the lab. What it is not is Google's answer.

choices.text: That it fits the provider's schema, and no more
choices.why: Right. A plan checks every field against the provider and contacts nobody; an organisation policy or a quota can still refuse it.

prompt: Which of these does the course mark as read rather than run? Choose all that apply.
hint: What has an emulator, and what only has documentation?

choices.text: Creating a project and moving it into a folder
choices.why: Right. No emulator answers the resource hierarchy; a plan describes it and the documentation says what Google does.

choices.text: A deny policy refusing a request
choices.why: Right. IAM is judged only by Google, and the emulator checks no permission.

choices.text: Publishing a message to a Pub/Sub topic
choices.why: The emulator answers this, so it is run.

choices.text: Google refusing a request that carries the placeholder token
choices.why: That one is run: the refusal comes from Google itself and is quoted as it arrived.

prompt: Why does the course leave Cloud Shell out as the lab, though it comes with `gcloud` installed?
hint: What does Cloud Shell need before it opens?

choices.text: It needs a Google account, and the course needs none
choices.why: Right. Lesson 23 is about Cloud Shell; it is not the lab, because opening it means having an account.

choices.text: It cannot run Java, so the emulator would not start
choices.why: That is not the reason the course gives. The obstacle comes before any program: the account.

choices.text: Its version of `gcloud` is too old for the lessons
choices.why: Cloud Shell carries a recent CLI. The version is not what keeps it out.

choices.text: It charges by the hour from the first minute
choices.why: The course gives a different reason, and it is not about money.

prompt: A lesson stops the emulator and starts it again before its first command. What does the restart give it?
hint: Where does the emulator keep what it is told?

choices.text: A new version of the emulator, downloaded on start
choices.why: The emulator is a component installed at the CLI's version. Starting it downloads nothing.

choices.text: The topics of the previous lesson, read back from a file
choices.why: It is the other way round: nothing the emulator was told survives a restart.

choices.text: An empty Pub/Sub: the emulator keeps it all in memory
choices.why: Right. Stopping it forgets every topic, so each lesson starts from nothing and a mistake costs nothing.

choices.text: A fresh placeholder token for the session
choices.why: The token is a file the setup wrote once, and the emulator ignores it anyway.

prompt: What would go wrong if `env.sh` left out `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG` on a laptop where somebody once ran `gcloud auth login` with a real account?
hint: Where does `gcloud` keep its settings when nothing says otherwise?

choices.text: The emulator would refuse to start
choices.why: The emulator does not read that variable to start. The danger is where the CLI's requests would go.

choices.text: Terraform would download its provider again for every directory
choices.why: That is what `TF_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` prevents, a different line of the file.

choices.text: The lab's commands could reach that real account's projects
choices.why: Right. Without the variable, `gcloud` reads `~/.config/gcloud`, where the real credential is.

choices.text: Nothing, since the placeholder token would still be used
choices.why: The token file is named in the lab's own settings directory. Without the variable, that directory is not read.

prompt: Which property sends Pub/Sub requests to port 8085 of your own computer?
hint: It names an address, and only for one API.

choices.text: `api_endpoint_overrides/pubsub`
choices.why: Right. It replaces Google's address for Pub/Sub, and every other API keeps its own.

choices.text: `auth/access_token_file`
choices.why: That one says which credential to send, not where to send it.

choices.text: `core/project`
choices.why: The project is part of the request's path, not its destination.

choices.text: `compute/region`
choices.why: The region decides where Compute Engine resources go, and has nothing to do with Pub/Sub's address.

prompt: Put the steps of the setup in the order the lesson runs them.
hint: A component can only be added to a CLI that is already there.
items: unpack the Google Cloud CLI into `~/.local`
start the emulator in the first terminal
trap: Setting the properties before writing `env.sh` is the slip: without `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG` they would land in `~/.config/gcloud`, the directory the lab keeps away from.

prompt: Match each line of `env.sh` to what it does.
hint: One of them protects a real account you may have.

pairs.right: gives `gcloud` a settings directory of its own
points the client libraries at the emulator
keeps one copy of the Google provider
stops Terraform asking about new versions

right_distractors: sends the placeholder token to Google

prompt: Components of the CLI are installed at the ___ of the CLI you already have, so the same archive always brings the same emulator.
hint: The number in the archive's name.

prompt: `gcloud pubsub topics list` asks you to run `gcloud auth login`. What is the right response in this lab?
hint: The lab has never held a credential, and is not supposed to.

choices.text: Run `gcloud auth login` with a personal Google account
choices.why: That signs a real account into the directory the lab exists to keep it away from.

choices.text: Restart the emulator, since it has lost the session
choices.why: The emulator keeps no session and was never asked. The CLI stopped before sending anything.

choices.text: Reinstall the CLI, because the archive was damaged
choices.why: A damaged CLI would not have printed a tidy message. It ran, and it ran without the lab's settings.

choices.text: Read `env.sh` into the terminal
choices.why: Right. Without `CLOUDSDK_CONFIG`, `gcloud` looked in `~/.config/gcloud` and found no placeholder token.

prompt: `gcloud crashed (ConnectionError)` ends with `Connection refused` on `localhost` port `8085`. What is missing?
hint: Who should be listening on that port?

choices.text: A Google account signed in to the CLI
choices.why: The request never left the laptop. A credential would not make a closed port answer.

choices.text: The emulator, which is not running
choices.why: Right. Nothing listens on 8085 until the emulator starts in the first terminal.

choices.text: The Java runtime
choices.why: Without Java the emulator refuses to start with a message of its own; this one is about a port nobody holds.

choices.text: A bug in `gcloud`, to report with `gcloud feedback`
choices.why: The word crashed is misleading here. The CLI behaved correctly with nobody to talk to.

prompt: A classmate's Pub/Sub command answers `UNAUTHENTICATED` and names `pubsub.googleapis.com`. What does that say about their lab?
hint: Which address answered, the laptop's or Google's?

choices.text: The override is missing, and the safety net did its job
choices.why: Right. The request went to Google, which refused the placeholder. Nothing happened in anybody's project.

choices.text: The emulator's IAM check refused the request
choices.why: The emulator checks no permission, and it would not answer under Google's address.

choices.text: The placeholder token has expired and needs writing again
choices.why: The word never expires because it was never valid. Google refuses it every time.

choices.text: Their real account lacks a role on `planner-dev`
choices.why: A missing role answers `PERMISSION_DENIED`. `UNAUTHENTICATED` means the credential itself was refused.

prompt: Put the first hour of a real account in the order the lesson gives.
hint: Protect, then limit, then work.
items: turn on two-step verification for the Google account
create a budget with alerts on the billing account
decide never to download a service account key
sign the CLI in, in a terminal that never reads `env.sh`
trap: Signing the CLI in first is the slip: until the account has a second factor and a budget, every credential handed out widens what a leaked password costs.

prompt: Why does the budget come before anything that can cost money, when a budget stops no spending?
hint: What does an alert give you, and when is it worth most?

choices.text: Google refuses to create resources in a project with no budget
choices.why: No such rule exists. A project with no budget creates resources and bills them.

choices.text: A budget switches the free tier on
choices.why: The free tier does not depend on a budget.

choices.text: An alert tells you while the amount is still small
choices.why: Right. It is a warning, not a brake, and a warning is worth most at the start.

choices.text: Spending past the budget is charged to Google instead
choices.why: Nothing moves the charge. Past the budget, the bill grows exactly as before.

prompt: What is `southamerica-east1-b`?
hint: Count the parts of the name.

choices.text: The second region in South America
choices.why: That is `southamerica-west1`, Santiago. A letter at the end marks a zone.

choices.text: A zone of the São Paulo region
choices.why: Right. The region's name with a letter on the end is one of its zones.

choices.text: A datacentre building in São Paulo
choices.why: A zone is a deployment area with its own power and network. Google does not say how many buildings it is.

choices.text: A backup copy of `southamerica-east1`
choices.why: Zones are not copies of a region. They are its parts, each able to fail alone.

prompt: Two teams in different companies plan around the same outage. One says `southamerica-east1-a` was down. Does the other know which zone that was?
hint: Does Google shuffle the letters between customers?

choices.text: No: each project maps the letters to zones at random
choices.why: That is another provider's arrangement. In Google Cloud the letters are not reshuffled.

choices.text: Only if both companies share one organisation
choices.why: The organisation has nothing to do with zone names. They are the same for everybody.

choices.text: Only after comparing zone ids in the console
choices.why: There is no separate zone id to compare. The name is enough.

choices.text: Yes: the name means the same zone to everybody
choices.why: Right. Google does not remap zone letters per customer, so the name is shared.

prompt: A user in Manaus reaches a service in São Paulo whose address is on Standard Tier. Where does the request join Google's network?
hint: Standard Tier hands the traffic to the public internet. For how much of the way?

choices.text: At the point of presence nearest Manaus
choices.why: That is Premium Tier, the default. The question says Standard.

choices.text: In Santiago, the other South American region
choices.why: Nothing routes a request for São Paulo through Santiago. It enters near the region it is for.

choices.text: Nowhere, as Standard Tier is the public internet end to end
choices.why: The region is Google's, so the request is inside Google's network by the time it arrives.

choices.text: Near the region, after crossing the public internet
choices.why: Right. Standard Tier gives up the backbone between the user and the region, in exchange for a lower price.

prompt: Google calls the default arrangement, in which traffic joins its backbone near the user, ___ Tier.
hint: The opposite of Standard.

prompt: At the prices read on 30 October 2026, what does a month of 800 GiB between two zones of `southamerica-east1` cost, in dollars?
hint: A cent per GiB.

prompt: A design replicates 300 GiB a month from São Paulo to Santiago. At the prices read on 30 October 2026, how many dollars more a month is that than the same 300 GiB between two US regions?
hint: 0.14 against 0.02, on the same volume.

prompt: Why does the course quote Google's network prices from the pricing page by hand, with a date, rather than from a downloaded price file?
hint: What does Google's machine-readable catalogue ask for?

choices.text: Google forbids copying its prices into a program of your own
choices.why: No such rule is the reason. The obstacle is the key the catalogue asks for.

choices.text: The Cloud Billing Catalog API needs an API key, which belongs to a project
choices.why: Right. With no account there is no project and no key, so the page is the source, and the date goes with each number.

choices.text: Network prices change every day
choices.why: They change, and that is why each carries a date; they do not change daily.

choices.text: The emulator can price Pub/Sub messages instead
choices.why: The emulator knows no price at all.

prompt: A team in São Paulo is choosing between two zones in `southamerica-east1` and a second region in Santiago for a database replica that receives 2,000 GiB a month. Going by the prices read on 30 October 2026, what does the choice cost?
hint: Multiply the volume by each price, then compare.

choices.text: The same in both, since the replica stays in South America
choices.why: From São Paulo, every other region costs 0.14, Santiago included. Staying on the continent saves nothing.

choices.text: Nothing in either case, because replication is internal traffic
choices.why: Only traffic inside one zone is free. Crossing a zone costs a cent per GiB.

choices.text: About 20 dollars across zones, about 280 across regions
choices.why: Right. 2,000 × 0.01 is 20 and 2,000 × 0.14 is 280: the second region costs fourteen times as much to feed.

choices.text: About 40 dollars a month across regions, as North America charges
choices.why: That is the US price of 0.02. Leaving São Paulo costs seven times more.
